idiom_name: structural typing at compile time; call-site type guards at runtime
implementation_notes: TypeScript interfaces are structural: an unrelated class satisfies an interface when its members line up, with no implements clause and no base type, and the compiler erases every interface, alias and generic at build time, so the runtime sees plain JavaScript. One declared type therefore holds unrelated implementations, and recovering a narrower type afterwards is a user-defined type guard or a discriminated union - not instanceof, which cannot see an interface that no longer exists. Where the type set is closed, a discriminated union with an exhaustive switch is the self-documenting alternative and needs no erasure at all.
pitfalls: Interfaces are erased: instanceof and typeof cannot test for them, so write a type guard or put a discriminating tag on the value when a runtime decision is required.

Structural typing is silent about intent: two unrelated types with the same members are interchangeable, so a wrong-but-compatible value compiles - add a unique-symbol brand when confusion is possible.
as-assertions (v as Drawable) bypass the check entirely; prefer unknown plus a guard, and remember excess-property checking does not apply through a variable.
